clue.text: Observation from persistent inquisitor? That's more like it!

definitions.meaning: read literally, a remark from an interrogator whose silent captive has finally started to speak
an idiom of approval when someone at last says what you hoped to hear

explanation.definitionFit: Both readings fit: a literal remark from an interrogator and the idiom of approval meaning an offer has become acceptable.

clue.text: See 5
Elegant thing with old tie, we hear, and whip

parts.note: tie sounds like Thai, and an old word for Thai (from Siam, Thailand's former name) is Siamese
the cat-o'-nine-tails is a whip, often shortened to cat

explanation.surface: A dandy's outfit lists an old school tie and a riding whip.
explanation.walkthrough: The sound of 'tie' gives Thai, and 'old' sends it back to Siam, the country's former name. The cat (o'-nine-tails) was a flogging whip.
explanation.definitionFit: The Siamese breed is famed for its sleek, graceful build, so an elegant creature describes it well.

clue.text: Out of curiosity, one's raised by English twins ordered on line

indicators.note: ordered means put into a new arrangement, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
two copies of E, the abbreviation for English
a row is a line of things side by side

explanation.surface: A remark about twins standing in a queue with a raised look of curiosity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' looks like a link word but is part of the pool that 'ordered' rearranges; 'on' just places the line after it.
explanation.definitionFit: People lift a brow when puzzled or inquisitive, so a curious person raises this facial feature.

clue.text: African nation resembling an audience who are receptive to race

parts.note: Togo is a country in West Africa
resembling means like
a receptive audience applauds, so its members are the clappers

explanation.surface: An African country is praised as a crowd that welcomes a race.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'go like the clappers' is British for moving very fast; the clappers here are applauding spectators.
explanation.definitionFit: The British idiom means to move at great speed, a colourful way of saying run flat out.

clue.text: Quiet solver was man in Telegraph having a lovely time?

indicators.note: in places the run of pieces inside the word for the telegraph

parts.note: to wire is to send a telegram, and a wire is a telegraph message
sh is the call for quiet
the solver is you, the reader
were is a past form of be, matching was
he stands for a man

explanation.surface: A hushed puzzle-solver once worked at the Telegraph newspaper and enjoyed every moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Telegraph' looks like the newspaper but means a telegram's medium, split open by 'in' after its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The stock phrase written on holiday postcards follows the line about having a lovely time.

clue.text: One bearing another's responsibility put out, about to argue right when wrong

indicators.note: about means going round, so the word for put out encloses the rest

parts.note: to smother a fire is to put it out

indicators.note: when wrong means the letters are arranged wrongly, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Someone takes on another's burden, irritated, about to quarrel about what's right when things go wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put out' reads as annoyed but means extinguished; 'about' wraps that word round the rearranged letters, opening after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: She carries a pregnancy for another person, literally bearing a child that is someone else's responsibility.

clue.text: Talentless, without a virtue

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the letter named next is taken away

parts.note: having no ability, as a two-word phrase

explanation.surface: Someone lacking any skill is also lacking any good quality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes the A from NO ABILITY; 'a' is the letter dropped, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Nobility of character is a moral excellence, the high-mindedness of a noble soul.

clue.text: Hateful, bespectacled princess, American

parts.note: Princess Di framed by a pair of round spectacles, drawn as two Os around her
US abbreviates the United States, so American

explanation.surface: A spiteful description of a royal in glasses from the States.
explanation.walkthrough: The two lenses of spectacles are pictured as O and O placed around DI (Princess Diana).
explanation.definitionFit: Something odious arouses hatred or disgust, a close synonym for hateful.

clue.text: My clue to rock concerts here

indicators.note: to rock means to shake about, so the letters of the preceding words are mixed up

explanation.surface: The setter boasts that his clue leads to a rock music venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to rock' rearranges MYCLUE. The Lyceum is a London theatre long used for rock concerts.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lyceum in London is a famous venue that has hosted rock gigs and other concerts.

clue.text: Booklet, little book on fish gutted alongside river

parts.note: B is a short form of book

indicators.note: gutted means the insides are removed, so the middle letter goes

parts.note: the roach is a freshwater fish
the Ure is a river in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: A small book about a cleaned fish sits beside a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gutted' removes A, the middle of ROACH, leaving ROCH. 'on' and 'alongside' simply put the pieces in order.
explanation.definitionFit: A brochure is a small pamphlet or booklet, usually advertising something.

clue.text: Plant 5 2

definitions.meaning: a marsh plant with hollow stems used for mats and chair seats
the linked phrase at 5 and 2 down means to move at great speed

explanation.definitionFit: The word names a waterside grass-like plant and also means to hurry or dash.

clue.text: Road clearer today, parking in shed

indicators.note: in places the two pieces before it inside the word for shed

parts.note: a snake will slough its skin, i.e. shed it
now means at the present time

explanation.surface: A gritter is parked in a shed today ready to clear the roads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shed' looks like a garden hut but is the verb, cast off skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A snowplough is a vehicle that pushes snow off roads to clear them.

clue.text: Support playwright about one part

parts.note: a prop is a support

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the playwright goes round the letter for one

parts.note: Joe Orton was an English playwright
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Backing a dramatist in roughly a single section of his work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' places ORTON around I. Joe Orton wrote Loot and Entertaining Mr Sloane.
explanation.definitionFit: A proportion is a share or part of a whole.

clue.text: Bird to use beak set about Old Bill first

indicators.note: set about means placed around, so the word for using a beak encloses the rest

parts.note: a bird uses its beak to peck

indicators.note: first tells us the word bill goes before the word old

parts.note: AC is the abbreviation for account, a bill

explanation.surface: A bird about to peck at a policeman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old Bill' looks like British slang for the police, but it splits into two abbreviations, and 'first' puts the bill ahead of old.
explanation.definitionFit: The peacock is the male peafowl, a large bird known for its fanned tail.

clue.text: Comedian in part of theatre gets the birds

indicators.note: in places the comedian inside the part of the theatre

parts.note: the gods are the highest gallery of a theatre
a wit is a clever, funny person

explanation.surface: A comic in the upper gallery is given the bird by the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes a booed comic 'getting the bird'; the gods are the cheap top seats.
explanation.definitionFit: Godwits are long-billed wading birds of marshes and mudflats.

clue.text: Provoke with smoke

definitions.meaning: the fragrant smoke from burning spices or joss sticks

explanation.definitionFit: As a verb the word means to enrage, and as a noun it is aromatic fumes from burnt resin.

clue.text: US city an insect invades soon, I suspect

indicators.note: invades means enters, so the pieces before it go inside
suspect as an adjective suggests something is not as it seems, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: an ant is an insect

explanation.surface: Someone fears that an insect will soon overrun an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I suspect' reads as a hedge, but suspect (dubious) is the anagram signal and the I is fodder; the insect pair goes in after the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: San Antonio is a large city in Texas, home of the Alamo.

clue.text: European city travel spoken about

indicators.note: spoken about means said out loud, so we want a word that sounds like the synonym

parts.note: to roam is to travel widely

explanation.surface: Talk of travelling to a European capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Rome is the capital of Italy, a major European city.

clue.text: Vehicle has to veer across motorway

indicators.note: across tells us the first move goes over the next piece

parts.note: to skip is to jump or swerve suddenly
a motorway is divided into lanes

explanation.surface: A car is forced to swerve across the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'veer across motorway' as skip lane, hopping from one lane to another. A skiplane is an aircraft on skis.
explanation.definitionFit: A skiplane is an aircraft fitted with skis for landing on snow, a vehicle of the air.

clue.text: Vast number mad, losing head

indicators.note: losing head means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: barmy is British slang for crazy

explanation.surface: A huge crowd goes crazy and loses control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing head' removes the B from BARMY, British slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: An army can mean a huge crowd, as in an army of volunteers.

clue.text: Island a success during regular parts of trip

indicators.note: during means within, so the pieces go inside
regular parts means every other letter is taken

parts.note: a hit is a success

explanation.surface: A successful trip to a tropical island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regular parts of' picks T and I from trip; 'during' puts A+HIT between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Tahiti is the largest island of French Polynesia in the South Pacific.

clue.text: An orderly part of Northern Ireland

parts.note: trim means neat and orderly

explanation.surface: A tidy region of Northern Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'orderly' looks like a hospital attendant but is the adjective, trim.
explanation.definitionFit: Antrim is one of the six counties of Northern Ireland.

clue.text: Inflicts punishment as rushes around company

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the word for rushes encloses company

parts.note: surges means rushes forward

explanation.surface: A firm is engulfed by a stampede that punishes it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rushes' looks like the plants but is the verb, surges forward.
explanation.definitionFit: To scourge is to whip, so it inflicts severe punishment.
